Frontier models can now propose technical social science research designs that experts grade more highly than the world's top political economist's---that's the finding from our new Free Systems eval, SnyderBench, in which we have PhD experts blind grade research proposals from AI models compared to papers written by Harvard political economist Jim Snyder (which the experts have not previously read). 

At the same time, we see no evidence that models can develop research ideas that experts rate as better overall contributions. They're getting better and better at the technical part of research, but not necessarily at the more subjective part.

This could be because human experts possess "judgment" that the models do not. 

It could also be that research "contribution" is so subjective that it doesn't actually point at any meaningful goal---consistent with this possibility, we find that our human experts don't agree with one another when rating project ideas for the strength of their contribution, with agreement rates barely higher than random chance. Perhaps social science research is what @alexolegimas might call a "relational good": something people value in part because it's produced by a human. We're not sure. 

This past January, I released the results of a pilot in which I had Claude Code replicate and extend a past empirical paper on vote-by-mail. 10 months later, it's stunning the amount of progress that's been made. It's no longer interesting to ask whether AI can collect data and run analyses automagically---we take that for granted---instead, the question is how much of the entire research loop AI can complete. Our tentative answer: AI can handle the technical aspects of empirical political economy research from end to end, devising the design and executing it, but for now, we still need humans to drive the agenda. 

This is joint work with @AndyCWMyers, and is of course dedicated to my PhD advisor Jim Snyder, who remains the world's great empirical political economist, AI or no AI.

One boring but very consequential reason why models feel bad at non-verifiable tasks is they never put any effort into them.

Humans can take years writing a novel, or months thinking about a game spec - but ask a model and it will just spit something out. Same, I imagine, would apply to capabilities like research taste - if you ask Ilya or Karpathy for 10 research ideas, they might agonise for days, ask Claude and you get them in minutes at best. 

Models don't seems to have any sense of self-awareness if their subjective output is good or bad. Humans have a sense of when they should keep working on a subjective task to get it just right.

So now we have this dichotomy, ask Claude to solve a millennium prize problem and it might spend months working away at it. Ask it to formulate a new set of Millennium Prize Problems and it will slop something up in minutes. This feels closer to a mechanical failure that fundamental lack of capability. I bet if models could find a way of working for months at non-verifiable tasks productively the outputs would be just as impressive as as those that we get with verifiable tasks. Hope labs will fix this.

Big moment for Local AI!

running models locally always had one hard rule. if the weights didn't fit in GPU VRAM or unified memory, the model didn't work.

that rule is why running a 180B-class open model has meant buying a $10-20K workstation.

but this is about to change.

in the video below, i'm running Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B model, on an M4 Max with 64 GB of memory.

it runs in OpenCode at 56 tokens/sec, with a 2-bit quant and a 64k context.

this sounds impossible, but it works because of how today's open models are built.

they are sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. each layer holds many small sub-networks called experts, and a router picks only a few of them per token.

Qwen 3.8 Flash Next has 180B parameters, but only ~6B run on any given token. so ~97% of the model sits idle on every token, and local runners still kept all of it in VRAM.

SSD expert streaming fixes this. it keeps attention and the session's most-reused experts in fast GPU or unified memory.

everything else stays on the NVMe SSD, and the engine reads it only when the router picks it.

however, it's not as simple as it sounds. a naive version of SSD streaming crawls at a couple of tokens/sec, and there are four reasons why:

↳ a basic cache evicts experts the next few tokens need again.

↳ layer-by-layer disk reads leave the GPU and SSD waiting on each other.

↳ speculative decoding verifies several tokens at once, so each step touches more experts.

↳ long prompts flush the cache that decoding depends on.

Magnitude, an open-source inference engine launching today, solves all four together:

↳ it ranks experts by reuse and keeps the top ones in GPU memory, so most tokens never touch the disk.

↳ it peeks at upcoming tokens and prefetches their experts before the GPU stalls.

↳ it schedules direct NVMe reads across layers and bypasses OS swap entirely.

↳ during prefill, it reads each cold expert once per layer while the GPU computes, so long prompts don't wipe the hot cache.

streaming never writes to the SSD, so there's no flash wear. more RAM or VRAM still helps, since it keeps more experts hot.

on first launch, Magnitude profiles the hardware, predicts tokens/sec for each model before download, and tunes kernels for that exact chip. there are no flags to set.

it runs on Apple Silicon, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, or plain CPU, as a desktop app, CLI, or Docker image. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cline connect in one click, with an OpenAI-compatible API for everything else.

i think this is the biggest change to local inference since quantization. the limit on what runs at home moves from VRAM size to SSD speed.

a fast NVMe drive costs a fraction of a high-end GPU.

it's free, Apache 2.0 licensed, and fully local.

No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Neon just hand-wrote Qwen3-0.6B inference engines in RAW x86-64 machine code and BOTH beat llama.cpp.

Zero compilers. Zero assemblers. Just raw hex piped into xxd -r -p.

Opus squeezed it into 7,331 bytes. Neon hit 188.93 tok/s (+81.4%).

Both models worked in isolated sandboxes targeting a 48-core AMD EPYC 7642 without gcc, nasm, ld, or any script converting mnemonics into bytes. Every ELF64 header, VEX prefix, ModR/M byte, and jump offset went directly into engine.hex by hand.

Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh, Claude Code) finished first in 65 minutes with a 7,331-byte static ELF64. Using f32 activations, transparent hugepages, and CCX pinning, it hit 21.44 to 125.13 tok/s and beat llama.cpp by +10.4% to +28.9% across 1 to 40 threads, costing $21.40 across 175 turns.

Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh, Antigravity) took 103 minutes with a 10,752-byte binary, and went completely feral on the microarchitecture. Int8 activations missed 1 token by a 0.0005 logit margin, so Neon invented a per-block Q15 (int16) AVX2 dot kernel, pinned 15 weight layers (239.2 MiB) inside the 256 MiB victim L3 cache with hybrid prefetcht0 and prefetchnta instructions, and routed threads around an offline CPU core in the CCX map.

It hit 22.27 to 188.35 tok/s mean across 1 to 40 threads, peaking at 188.93 tok/s at 32 threads compared to llama.cpp at 103.82 tok/s. That is +81.4% faster than llama.cpp and 50% faster than Opus, for $16.72 across 90 turns.

Frontier models are now hand-writing raw VEX machine code faster than C++ for under $20, and both binaries are smaller than a compiled Hello World.

I proved my own math conjecture using AI, thereby also settling a math problem that had been open for 23 years.

In 2022, during my PhD, my co-author Thomas Lehéricy and I came up with a conjecture in probability theory that we couldn’t prove. It turns out that Martin Raič had already proposed a special case of this conjecture in 2003, the year I was born. As recently as this February, mathematicians were still publishing papers on closely related questions.

I finished my PhD without a proof or a counterexample, and I kept wondering whether our conjecture was true. Whenever a new AI model came out, I gave it the problem, hoping it would figure out if we were right.

Our conjecture was about the central limit theorem, a cornerstone of probability theory. If you toss a hundred fair coins independently, you get 50 heads on average. The exact number varies, and a bell curve gives a good estimate of how likely you are to get, say, between 45 and 55 heads. We wanted to know how accurate that approximation is when each outcome can depend on a few of the others. We published our conjecture and some partial results in 2024.

I gave the problem to several AI models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2. Those models made partial progress. GPT-6.2 Astra was the first to find a complete proof.

You can find the paper and the accompanying Lean formalization on GitHub below. I’ve also submitted the paper to arXiv and will share the arXiv link once it’s live, likely early next week.
